article.title: Why a Model Threshold Is a Business Decision, Not Just a Statistical One
article.why: Applied ML English for choosing thresholds using error costs, capacity, base rate, and business value.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
A classification model often produces a probability or score rather than a final yes-or-no decision. The threshold converts that score into an action. If the threshold is 0.5, a case with a predicted probability of 0.51 becomes positive and a case with 0.49 becomes negative. This looks objective, but the choice of threshold is not purely statistical. It determines who receives an action, how many cases a team must handle, and which kinds of mistakes the business accepts.

Suppose a fraud model scores 100,000 transactions. A low threshold catches more suspicious transactions, which can increase recall, but it also produces more false positives. If every positive case requires manual review, lowering the threshold may create more alerts than investigators can process. A threshold that looks attractive on an ROC curve can therefore fail operationally.

The cost of errors is another reason 0.5 is rarely a universal answer. In some problems, a false negative is expensive because missing a true case creates a large loss. In others, a false positive is costly because an unnecessary intervention harms customer experience or consumes scarce resources. The best threshold should reflect the relative cost of these errors, not only model accuracy.

Base rate matters as well. When positive cases are rare, even a model with good discrimination can generate many false positives. Imagine that only 1% of customers will respond to an offer. A threshold that selects half the population may achieve high recall but still waste most contacts. Precision, lift, expected value, and capacity can be more useful for deciding the operating point.

Business constraints can be translated into threshold rules. A marketing team may have budget for 200,000 messages, so it can choose the top-scoring 200,000 eligible customers rather than a fixed probability cutoff. A review team may be able to examine only 5,000 cases per week, so the threshold can be set to keep the alert volume near that limit. A lending process may need different thresholds for different risk bands because the financial exposure differs.

Thresholds should also be evaluated on data that resembles actual deployment. If the population changes, a threshold selected during development may produce a very different positive rate later. Monitoring should therefore include score distribution, selected volume, precision or proxy outcomes, and operational load. When those signals shift, the team may need to recalibrate the model, change the threshold, or investigate the data pipeline.

It is useful to separate three questions. First, how well does the model rank positive cases above negative ones? Metrics such as AUC can help answer this. Second, how well calibrated are the predicted probabilities? Calibration matters if a score of 0.2 is expected to mean roughly a 20% event rate. Third, what action should be taken at each score? That last question is where business value enters directly.

One practical method is to build a threshold table. For a range of candidate thresholds, calculate the number of selected cases, true positives, false positives, false negatives, precision, recall, and an estimated business value. Then add operational capacity and policy constraints. The chosen point should be explainable in those terms.

There may not be one permanent threshold. Different channels, customer segments, or seasons can have different economics. However, segment-specific thresholds should have a clear reason and should be governed carefully so that the process does not become impossible to monitor.

A model threshold is therefore a decision policy sitting on top of a prediction system. Statistics tell us what errors and trade-offs occur at each operating point. The business decides which trade-off is acceptable given costs, benefits, capacity, risk, and customer impact. Treating 0.5 as a default can be convenient during exploration, but treating it as the final business rule without analysis is usually a mistake.
